title: Will, arranged plans, could and obligation
matching: Typed answers ignore letter case, extra spaces, apostrophe style and final . ! or ? punctuation. Accents and every other character count. Multiple-choice answers must match exactly.

lessons.title: Will for predictions, offers and promises
lessons.explanation: Use will plus the base verb for simple predictions, quick offers and promises: It will be sunny tomorrow. I'll carry your bag. I won't be late. The short form is 'll and the negative is won't (will not). Will is the same for every subject and is never followed by to or by an -s form. Questions put will first: Will you help me?

lessons.title: Present continuous for arranged plans
lessons.explanation: Use am, is or are plus the -ing form for a fixed arrangement in the near future, usually with a future time: I'm meeting Anna on Friday. We're flying to Rome next week. Add a time expression so the sentence is clearly about the future. Questions put be first: Are you working tomorrow? Use going to for general intentions and the present continuous for a plan that already has a time or place.

lessons.title: Could for past ability and polite requests
lessons.explanation: Use could plus the base verb for general ability in the past: I could swim when I was five. The negative is couldn't (could not). Could is the same for every subject. Could also makes requests more polite: Could you open the window, please? Could I sit here? For one single past achievement use was able to or managed to, not could.

lessons.title: Must, have to and mustn't
lessons.explanation: Use must or have to for obligation: You must wear a seat belt. I have to get up early. Have to changes for the subject: she has to work. Use mustn't (must not) for prohibition: You mustn't smoke here. Do not confuse mustn't with don't have to: mustn't means it is forbidden, but don't have to means it is not necessary. Must is followed by the base verb with no to.

examples.en: You must wear a seat belt.
She has to work on Saturday.
